title: Redis for Caching, Sessions, Rate Limits, and Jobs
summary: Use Redis to cache reads, share sessions, limit request rates, run background jobs, and push live updates across every server.
intro: Once Roombook runs on several servers, anything one server keeps in its own memory stops working: a cached answer only one instance has, a login only one instance remembers, a request limit each instance counts on its own. The previous lesson said that kind of state has to move somewhere every instance can reach. For data that's small, read often, and fine to rebuild, that place is usually **Redis**, an in-memory store every instance shares. This lesson starts with what a cache is and why an API wants one, then teaches Redis and uses it from Spring Boot with Spring Data Redis: caching the availability endpoint and keeping that cache correct, sharing sessions, limiting request rates, running background jobs, and pushing live updates through every instance.

steps.title: Caches, and what Redis is
steps.body:
Some requests ask the same question over and over. In Roombook, `GET /v1/rooms/{roomId}/availability?date=2026-10-05` is by far the busiest endpoint: every student checks it before booking, and the display outside each room asks again every minute. Each request runs the same query and builds the same answer, until somebody books. A cache lets the API do that work once and hand out the result many times.

## What a cache is

A **cache** is a copy of an answer, kept somewhere fast, so the next request with the same question gets the copy instead of the work being done again. You met caches in the web course: a DNS resolver keeps each lookup for its TTL, and a browser keeps the files `Cache-Control` allows. A server-side cache is the same idea one layer further in. The API keeps answers it built from the database.

Every cache comes with a few words:

- A **hit** is a request the cache could answer. A **miss** is one it couldn't, so the real work happens, and its result is usually saved for next time.
- The **hit rate** is the share of requests that hit. At 95%, only one request in twenty reaches the database.
- A copy is **stale** when the real data changed after the copy was made. Every cache serves some stale answers, and designing one means deciding how stale is acceptable, and for how long.
- A **TTL**, time to live, is how long a copy may be kept before it's thrown away, the same word as in DNS.
- **Eviction** is the cache throwing copies out to make room, usually the ones used least recently.

Why bother? A hit costs a fraction of a millisecond, and the availability query costs a few milliseconds of database time. The database is the one piece every instance shares, so it's the first to run out of room as traffic grows. Taking repeated reads off it leaves room for the writes, which have to go there.

## Where the copy lives

The simplest cache is a variable in your server's memory: a `ConcurrentHashMap` in a bean, or a library like Caffeine. Every thread in one JVM shares it, but the next instance is another JVM with a cache of its own. That's fine for data that never changes, like a list of time zones. For anything else, it breaks as soon as there's more than one instance, which the previous lesson made the normal case.

```diagram redis-shared-cache
Each instance's memory holds its own copy. A shared cache holds one copy for all of them.
```

On the left, each instance keeps its own copy. A booking that arrives through instance 1 can clear instance 1's copy, but instances 2 and 3 never hear about it and keep handing out the old availability until their copies expire. Each one also misses on its own, so the database does the same work three times. On the right, all three read and clear the same copies in one shared store, so one booking clears the copy for everyone.

## Redis

**Redis** is that shared store, and the one most teams reach for. The name is short for Remote Dictionary Server. It's a server program, like PostgreSQL, that keeps **keys** and their **values** in memory and answers commands over the network on port 6379. Working from memory instead of disk is why a command usually takes well under a millisecond.

Three things about how it works shape everything this lesson does with it:

- **One command runs at a time.** Commands from every instance wait in line, and each finishes before the next starts. So every command is **atomic**: it happens completely or not at all, and nothing sees it halfway. Two instances that add 1 to the same counter at the same moment always end at 2, never at 1.
- **Any key can expire.** Give a key a TTL and Redis deletes it when the time is up. Caches, sessions, and rate limits all lean on that.
- **Memory is the limit.** Redis holds what fits in its memory. Set a `maxmemory` size and an eviction policy like `allkeys-lru`, which evicts the least recently used keys, and a full Redis throws old copies out instead of refusing new ones.

Redis can also save its data to disk, as a **snapshot** every few minutes or by appending every write to the **AOF**, the append-only file, so a restart doesn't wipe it. A pure cache can skip both, since anything lost is rebuilt from PostgreSQL, while sessions and job queues want the AOF turned on. Even then, keep the facts that matter, like bookings and users, in PostgreSQL.

In 2024 Redis changed its license, and the Linux Foundation started **Valkey**, a copy of Redis that keeps the old open-source license. Redis 8 went back to an open-source license in 2025. Both speak the same commands, so everything in this lesson works with either.

## Keys

A key is a string, built from parts joined by colons, from general to specific: `roombook:availability:1:2026-10-05` is the availability of room 1 on October 5. The `roombook:` prefix keeps Roombook's keys apart from any other app's on the same Redis, and the rest makes each key easy to find and to delete by its pattern. To try the commands in the example, start Redis with `docker run --rm -p 6379:6379 redis:8` (the lesson on deploying explains Docker) and use `redis-cli`, Redis's own command-line client, in a second terminal.

examples.title: Strings, expiry, and counters
examples.prompt: With Redis running on your computer, cache an answer for 60 seconds, read it back, count twice, and delete. Each line runs one command through `redis-cli`.
examples.code:
redis-cli SET roombook:availability:1:2026-10-05 '{"roomId":1,"date":"2026-10-05","freeSlots":[]}' EX 60
redis-cli GET roombook:availability:1:2026-10-05
redis-cli TTL roombook:availability:1:2026-10-05
redis-cli INCR roombook:demo:visits
redis-cli INCR roombook:demo:visits
redis-cli DEL roombook:availability:1:2026-10-05
redis-cli GET roombook:availability:1:2026-10-05
examples.explanation: Each command prints one short answer. `SET` stores the JSON as a string, and `EX 60` gives it a TTL of 60 seconds in the same step, so Redis answers `OK`. `GET` returns the string exactly as stored, since Redis never looks inside a value. `TTL` answers with the seconds left, like `57`, counting down to `-2` once the key is gone (`-1` means a key with no TTL). `INCR` reads the value as a whole number and adds 1. A key that doesn't exist counts as 0, so the first `INCR` answers `1` and the second `2`. `DEL` answers `1`, the number of keys it deleted, and the last `GET` answers `(nil)`, Redis's word for no value.

steps.title: Data types and the client
steps.body:
A Redis value isn't always a string. Each key holds one **data type**, and each type comes with commands that change it inside Redis, in one atomic step. That's the point: your code never has to read a value, change it, and write it back while another instance does the same. Picking the right type is most of designing with Redis.

| Type | What it holds | Commands | Typical uses |
|---|---|---|---|
| String | text, bytes, or a number, up to 512 MB | `SET`, `GET`, `INCR`, `MGET` | cached JSON, counters, locks |
| Hash | an object: named fields with values | `HSET`, `HGET`, `HGETALL`, `HINCRBY` | sessions, settings |
| List | an ordered list, pushed and popped at both ends | `LPUSH`, `RPOP`, `BLMOVE`, `LRANGE` | simple queues, recent items |
| Set | unique strings, in no order | `SADD`, `SREM`, `SISMEMBER`, `SMEMBERS` | tags, ids already seen |
| Sorted set | unique strings, each ordered by a number | `ZADD`, `ZRANGE`, `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` | leaderboards, rate limits |
| Stream | an append-only log that groups of workers read | `XADD`, `XREADGROUP`, `XACK` | background jobs, event logs |

Every type can expire: `EXPIRE key 60` gives any key a TTL, and `SET` takes `EX` to store a value and its TTL in one step. A command on a key that doesn't exist treats it as empty, so `INCR` starts a counter at 0 and `SADD` creates the set. Commands also check types: `INCR` on a hash fails with a `WRONGTYPE` error.

## More than one command

Each command is atomic, but often you need two in a row, like adding 1 to a counter and then setting its TTL. Redis gives you three ways to send several:

- A **pipeline** sends many commands without waiting for each answer, then reads all the answers. It saves round trips, but other clients' commands can run in between yours.
- A **transaction** is `MULTI`, then the commands, then `EXEC`. Redis queues them and runs them back to back, with nothing from anyone else in between.
- A **Lua script**, sent with `EVAL`, is a small program that runs inside Redis as one atomic step. **Lua** is a small programming language built into Redis. Unlike a transaction, a script can read a value and decide what to write next. The rate limit later in this lesson uses one.

## Connecting from Spring Boot

Add `spring-boot-starter-data-redis`. It brings **Spring Data Redis**, Spring's layer over Redis, and **Lettuce**, the client underneath it. Set `spring.data.redis.url` in `application.yaml`, taken from `REDIS_URL` in the environment, as the example shows, and Boot builds the connection and a `StringRedisTemplate` bean, which you take in a constructor like any other bean.

Lettuce shares one connection between all threads and **multiplexes** it: commands from every request go down it in order, and the answers come back in the same order, which Redis guarantees. So there's no pool to size.

A few choices matter:

- **`StringRedisTemplate`, not `RedisTemplate`.** It stores keys and values as plain strings, so you decide how objects become JSON, with the `JsonMapper` Boot already configured, and anyone reading Redis by hand sees readable text. The plain `RedisTemplate` uses Java serialization by default, which stores binary that only Java can read, and that breaks when a class changes.
- **Commands are grouped by type:** `opsForValue()` for strings, then `opsForHash()`, `opsForList()`, `opsForSet()`, `opsForZSet()`, and `opsForStream()`.
- **Set `spring.data.redis.timeout`.** Lettuce waits up to a minute for an answer by default, so a Redis outage would hold each request that long. Half a second is plenty, and the next parts decide what a failure means. For a cache, it means ask PostgreSQL.

examples.title: Hashes, lists, sets, and sorted sets
examples.prompt: Try one command of each of the other types. These `demo` keys are only for trying things.
examples.code:
redis-cli HSET roombook:demo:user:1 name Ada role member
redis-cli HGET roombook:demo:user:1 role
redis-cli LPUSH roombook:demo:queue job-1 job-2
redis-cli RPOP roombook:demo:queue
redis-cli SADD roombook:demo:seen evt-41 evt-42 evt-41
redis-cli SISMEMBER roombook:demo:seen evt-42
redis-cli ZADD roombook:demo:bookings 12 lovelace 30 turing 7 hopper
redis-cli ZRANGE roombook:demo:bookings 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
examples.explanation: `HSET` sets two fields of a hash and answers `2`, the number of new fields, and `HGET` answers `member`. `LPUSH` adds both jobs at the left end and answers `2`, the list's length. `RPOP` takes from the right end, so it answers `job-1`, the first one pushed: pushing on one end and popping from the other makes a first-in, first-out queue. `SADD` answers `2`, since `evt-41` twice is still one member, and `SISMEMBER` answers `1`, meaning yes. `ZADD` adds three rooms, each scored with a number of bookings. `ZRANGE ... REV WITHSCORES` lists them highest first, each followed by its score: `turing` and `30`, then `lovelace` and `12`, then `hopper` and `7`.

examples.title: Pointing Boot at Redis
examples.prompt: `src/main/resources/application.yaml`, with the Redis settings. The `${...}` reads an environment variable, with a default after the colon.
examples.explanation: `url` names the server, and the default after the colon is Redis on your own computer, so a developer needs no setup while production sets `REDIS_URL`. A URL can also carry a password and a database number, like `redis://:secret@cache.internal:6379/0`, and `rediss://` with two s's turns on TLS. `timeout` is how long a command waits for its answer. With these two lines, Boot creates the Lettuce connection, a `StringRedisTemplate` bean, and a health indicator that Actuator reports, and any bean can take the template in its constructor.

steps.title: Caching reads with cache-aside
steps.body:
Roombook's availability endpoint is the one to cache first. It's read constantly, it's the same for everyone who asks about the same room and day, and a slightly old answer does no harm, for a reason this part ends on. The pattern nearly every API uses for it is **cache-aside**: the cache sits beside the database, and your code checks it first.

## Cache-aside, step by step

```diagram redis-cache-aside
On a hit, Redis answers and PostgreSQL is never asked. On a miss, the answer is built once and saved.
```

1. The service builds the key from the request, `roombook:availability:1:2026-10-05`, and asks Redis for it with `GET`.
2. On a **hit**, Redis returns the saved JSON, the service turns it back into an object, and the request is done. PostgreSQL never hears about it.
3. On a **miss**, Redis returns nothing, so the service runs the real query against PostgreSQL.
4. It saves the result with `SET` and a TTL, so the next request for that room and day is a hit, and returns it.

It's also called lazy loading, because nothing is cached until someone asks, so the cache fills with exactly what people use. The main alternative, **write-through**, writes to the cache on every change instead. That keeps it warm, but it caches plenty nobody reads and gives every write a second job.

## The choices inside it

**What to store.** Store the finished answer, the JSON the endpoint returns, not raw rows. A hit should cost one `GET` and one parse, nothing more.

**How long to keep it.** The TTL is the longest a stale answer can live. Availability gets 60 seconds: long enough that a busy room's display and its visitors share one query a minute, and short enough that a missed update fixes itself quickly. Data that rarely changes, like a building's opening hours, can keep an hour.

**What a failure means.** Redis can be down or slow, and a cache must never take the API down with it. If the `GET` fails, log it and go to PostgreSQL as if it were a miss. If the `SET` fails, log it and return the answer anyway. The request gets slower, not broken. That's why the previous part set a short `timeout`: an outage should cost each request half a second at most.

**Keys that tell users apart.** Availability is the same for everyone, so its key needs only the room and the date. Anything that depends on who's asking, like a user's own bookings, must have the user's id in its key, or one user gets another's answer.

## In Spring Boot

The example is `AvailabilityService` in the `rooms` package. It writes the answer as JSON with Boot's `JsonMapper` and reads it back the same way. Both Redis calls catch their own failures, log them, and carry on, so an outage only costs speed.

## The cache never decides

There's one more reason availability is safe to cache. The cache only tells students which slots look free. Booking still goes through `POST /v1/bookings`, which writes to PostgreSQL, where the exclusion constraint from the data integrity lesson refuses an overlap. So the worst a stale copy can do is show a slot that was taken a few seconds ago, and the booking answers 409 `booking-overlap`. Follow that rule everywhere: a cache can speed up what people see, but every decision that must be right reads the source of truth.

examples.title: The availability service
examples.prompt: `AvailabilityService` in the `rooms` package. The controller calls `availability.get(roomId, date)`.
examples.explanation: `get` follows the diagram: build the key, try Redis, and on a miss compute, save, and return. Spring Data Redis turns every Redis failure into a `DataAccessException`, the same family JDBC errors belong to, so one `catch` covers a refused connection and a timeout alike. `set(key, value, TTL)` sends `SET` with `EX` in one command. Jackson 3's `readValue` and `writeValueAsString` throw unchecked exceptions, so there's no `throws` clause. Later in the lesson, Spring's caching annotations write all of this for you, once you know what they do.

steps.title: Keeping a cache correct
steps.body:
A cache that's fast and wrong is worse than no cache. An old joke says there are only two hard things in computer science, cache invalidation and naming things, and this part is about the first: making sure a change in PostgreSQL reaches the copies in Redis, and that the cache holds up in the moment it matters most.

## Delete the copy after the commit

**Invalidation** means removing a copy once it's wrong. When a booking is created or cancelled, the availability for that room and day changes, so the bookings service deletes that one key, and the next read builds a fresh copy. The day is the booking's date in the building's time zone, the same date the availability endpoint takes.

Two details make it reliable:

- **Delete, don't update.** Writing the new availability into Redis yourself means computing it during the write, and two writes close together can save their answers in the wrong order, leaving the older one in the cache. A delete can't land out of order: whatever happens, the next read rebuilds from PostgreSQL.
- **Delete after the commit, not before.** Delete inside the transaction, and a read can slip in between the delete and the commit, see the old data, and cache it again. Deleting after the commit, the after-commit hook from the data integrity lesson, closes that gap.

A small window is left: if the instance crashes between the commit and the delete, the old copy survives. That's what the TTL is for. It's the safety net that heals every missed delete within 60 seconds. A failed delete is logged, not returned as an error, since the booking itself succeeded.

In Spring, the bookings service publishes a `BookingConfirmed` event inside its `@Transactional` method, and a `@TransactionalEventListener` with `phase = AFTER_COMMIT` evicts the key, as the second example shows. Spring calls it only once the transaction has committed, and never after a rollback.

## Stampedes

A popular key expires, and in the next millisecond 300 requests miss at once. All 300 run the same query, and the database gets a burst of identical work, often when it's busiest. That's a **cache stampede**, also called a thundering herd. Three habits prevent it:

- **Coalesce requests.** While a miss is being filled, later requests for the same key wait for that one result instead of starting their own. In Spring, `@Cacheable(sync = true)` does it for you, as the first example shows.
- **Add jitter to TTLs.** Keys cached at the same moment, say right after a deploy, also expire at the same moment. Adding a few random seconds to each TTL spreads them out.
- **Lock across instances when the work is expensive.** Coalescing works inside one process, so ten instances can still run a query ten times. For a report that takes seconds to build, the first instance takes a short lock with `SET key token NX PX 5000` (set only if the key doesn't exist, and expire in 5,000 milliseconds), builds the value, and the others wait briefly and read the cache.

A Redis lock is a fine way to avoid duplicate work, and the wrong way to protect correctness. It expires on a timer, so a process that pauses longer than the lock lasts, in a long garbage collection or a slow network, can wake up and carry on while someone else holds the lock too. When two writers must never overlap, like two bookings for one slot, let the database decide with a constraint or a row lock.

## What not to cache

- **What must be exactly right at that moment:** the booking decision, a permission check just after an admin removes a role.
- **What's different for every request**, like a free-text search. The hit rate is near zero, so the cache only adds a round trip.
- **What's already cheap.** Reading one row by its primary key takes a fraction of a millisecond, and a cache in front of it adds a second system for nothing.
- **Large values.** A value of several megabytes ties Redis up while it's sent, and Redis runs one command at a time.

Before you add a cache, make the query fast with the right index. A cache hides a slow query until the day the cache is empty, and then the slow query is all you have.

examples.title: The same cache with Spring's annotations
examples.prompt: `AvailabilityService` rewritten with Spring's cache abstraction. A configuration class with `@EnableCaching` points the `availability` cache at Redis, with JSON values and a TTL.
examples.explanation: `@Cacheable` wraps the method in a proxy that does cache-aside: it builds a key from the expression, here `1:2026-10-05`, tries the cache, and calls the method only on a miss, saving what it returns. `sync = true` coalesces: while one thread fills a key, other threads asking for it wait for that result. `@CacheEvict` deletes the key. The configuration class sets the TTL to 60 seconds plus a random 0 to 9, stores values as JSON, and prefixes keys, so the full key is `roombook:availability::1:2026-10-05`. It has the trap the data integrity lesson showed for `@Transactional`: a call from inside the same class skips the proxy, so evict from another bean.

examples.title: Evicting after the commit
examples.prompt: `BookingCacheListener` in the `bookings` package. The bookings service publishes `BookingConfirmed` inside its transaction, as in the data integrity lesson, and the event now carries the room and the times too.
examples.explanation: `@TransactionalEventListener` holds the event until the transaction ends, and `phase = AFTER_COMMIT` runs this method only if it committed. A rollback, say from the exclusion constraint, drops the event, which is right, since nothing changed. `LocalDate.ofInstant` turns the booking's start into its date in New York, where both buildings are, which is the date the availability key uses. The listener calls `evict` on the service bean, so the call goes through the proxy and `@CacheEvict` works. If Redis is down, Spring logs the exception and the booking still succeeds, since it already committed.

steps.title: Sessions and rate limits
steps.body:
Two kinds of state from earlier lessons get faster and simpler in Redis: the sessions that keep users signed in, and the counters that limit how often a caller may ask.

## Sessions every instance can read

The authentication lesson kept sessions in PostgreSQL, in Spring Session JDBC's `SPRING_SESSION` table: a random id in the `__Host-session` cookie, and a row on the server with the user and an expiry. That works on any number of instances, since they share the database, but it costs a query on every signed-in request, and expired rows stay until a cleanup job deletes them. Redis fits sessions better:

- **The lookup is one command**, well under a millisecond.
- **Expiry is built in.** Store each session with a TTL, like Roombook's 7 days, and Redis deletes it when the time is up, with nothing to clean up.
- **Sliding expiry is one command.** Most sites sign you out after 30 minutes of doing nothing, not 30 minutes after you signed in, so each request pushes the expiry back. `GETEX key EX 1800` reads a session and resets its TTL in one step.
- **Logout is `DEL`**, and it takes effect on every instance at once.

The cookie and its flags stay exactly as they were. The same idea gives JWTs a way out: an access token can't be taken back once it's issued, so to revoke one early, put its id, the `jti` claim, in a **denylist** key whose TTL ends when the token does, and check for that key on each request.

Moving sessions into Redis makes Redis matter more: if it's down, nobody is signed in. Turn on the AOF so a restart keeps sessions, and answer a Redis outage with 503, not as if the user had signed out.

In Spring, sessions come from Spring Session, and moving them is a dependency swap: replace Spring Session JDBC with `spring-boot-starter-session-data-redis`, then set the timeout and the key namespace, as the first example shows. Spring Session stores each session as a Redis hash, resets its TTL on every request, and keeps `HttpSession` and the security context working exactly as before. Its keys hold the session id itself, so keep Redis on a private network with a password, as you would the database.

## Rate limits

A **rate limit** caps how many requests a caller may make in a span of time, and answers the rest with `429 Too Many Requests`. It protects the login endpoint from password guessing, the API from a client stuck in a loop, and the database from both. The counts must be shared: with three instances behind a load balancer, a limit each instance counts on its own lets three times as many through.

There are three common ways to count:

- A **fixed window** counts requests in each clock window, say 10 logins per caller from 09:00 to 09:15, then starts over. It's one counter per caller per window, the cheapest there is. Its flaw is at the edges: a caller can send 10 at 09:14 and 10 more at 09:15.
- A **sliding window** counts the requests in the 15 minutes before now, whenever now is, so the edges can't be gamed. Kept exactly, it's a sorted set of request times per caller, trimmed with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`.
- A **token bucket** gives each caller a bucket that refills at a steady rate, say one token a second up to 20, and each request spends one. It allows short bursts and a steady average, which suits scripts that call an API.

```diagram redis-rate-windows
Twenty requests around 09:15: the fixed window lets all of them through, and the sliding window refuses half.
```

A fixed window in Redis is two commands, `INCR` on the caller's counter for this window and an expiry the first time. They must run as one, or a crash between them leaves a counter that never expires, so they go in a small Lua script:

```text
local count = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if count == 1 then
  redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
end
return count
```

`KEYS[1]` is the counter, like `roombook:rl:login:203.0.113.7:1790845200`: the limit's name, the caller, and the window's start in Unix seconds. `ARGV[1]` is the window's length in seconds. When the count passes the limit, the API answers 429 with a `Retry-After` header holding the seconds until the window ends, in the same Problem Details format as every other error. An IETF draft adds `RateLimit-Policy` and `RateLimit` headers, which tell clients their quota on every response, before they hit it.

In Spring, the limit is a `OncePerRequestFilter` for the login path, as the second example shows. When you need token buckets or several limits per route, Bucket4j adds them, with Redis as its storage.

**Who is the caller?** Signed-in requests are limited by user id, and API keys by key, since one IP address can be a whole campus behind one router. Login has no user yet, so it's limited by IP address, and by the email being tried. Behind a load balancer, the address comes from `X-Forwarded-For`, trusted only from your own proxy, as the previous lesson explained. **If Redis is down**, most APIs fail open, letting requests through rather than refusing everyone.

examples.title: Spring Session on Redis
examples.prompt: `application.yaml`, after replacing Spring Session JDBC with `spring-boot-starter-session-data-redis` in `pom.xml`.
examples.code:
spring:
  session:
    timeout: 7d
    data:
      redis:
        namespace: roombook:session
examples.explanation: With the starter on the classpath, Boot replaces the servlet container's in-memory sessions with Redis ones, using the connection from the Redis settings. `timeout: 7d` is the same 7 days the authentication lesson set: how long a session lives after its last request. Spring Session resets that on every request, which is the sliding expiry. `namespace` prefixes the keys, so a session lives at `roombook:session:sessions:` plus its id, as a hash holding its creation time, last access time, and attributes. Your code doesn't change: the login saves the security context in the `HttpSession` as before, and logout invalidates it.

examples.title: A fixed-window limit as a filter
examples.prompt: `LoginRateLimitFilter` in the `common` package. As a `@Component`, Boot registers it with the servlet container, and `@Order(-101)` puts it just before Spring Security's chain at -100, as the middleware lesson explained, so it runs before any password check.
examples.explanation: `shouldNotFilter` skips every path but login. `windowStart` rounds the time down to the start of the current window, and the key names the limit, the caller, and that window. `RedisScript.of` wraps the Lua code with its result type, and `execute` sends it by its SHA-1 hash, falling back to the full text the first time. Past the limit, the filter writes a 429 with `Retry-After` and a `ProblemDetail` body itself, since a filter runs outside the controllers' exception handling, and never calls `chain.doFilter`. `getRemoteAddr` is the caller once `server.forward-headers-strategy` is set behind a proxy.

steps.title: Background jobs and live updates
steps.body:
Some work doesn't belong in a request. When Ada books a room, she should get a confirmation email, but the email provider takes a second to answer, sometimes ten, and now and then it's down. If `POST /v1/bookings` waits for it, Ada waits too, and a broken email provider breaks booking. So the request records that an email needs sending and answers, and a separate process sends it. That's a **background job**, run by a worker, the separate process the scaling-out lesson sketched.

## A queue between them

The API and the worker meet at a queue, as in the scaling-out lesson: the API adds a job, and a worker takes it and does it. The queue lives outside both, so jobs survive a restart of either, and any instance can add a job that any worker takes. Redis gives you two ways to build one:

- A **list**: `LPUSH` adds a job and `BRPOP` takes one, waiting until there is one. It's simple, but once a worker pops a job, Redis forgets it, so a worker that crashes halfway loses the job.
- A **stream**: `XADD` appends a job to a log, and workers read it through a **consumer group**, which tracks which worker has which job. A job a worker has read but not finished stays **pending** until the worker **acknowledges** it with `XACK`. If the worker dies, the job stays pending, and another worker can claim it with `XAUTOCLAIM` once it's been idle too long.

Use a stream for anything you'd mind losing, which is most jobs. Roombook's email jobs go in the stream `roombook:jobs:email`, read by the consumer group `email`. The `AFTER_COMMIT` listener that sent the email in the data integrity lesson now only adds a job to the stream: `XADD roombook:jobs:email * type booking-confirmed bookingId 1001`, which takes a millisecond.

## Jobs that can run twice

Acknowledging after the work, not before, means a job is never lost. It also means a job can run twice: if the worker sends the email and crashes before `XACK`, the next worker sends it again. That's **at-least-once delivery**, and the next lesson builds on it. For now, three rules:

- **Make jobs safe to run twice.** Before sending, check whether this booking's email already went out, or give the email provider the job's id so it drops a repeat.
- **Put ids in jobs, not data.** The job says `bookingId: 1001`, and the worker loads the booking when it runs, so it sends what's true then, and skips a booking cancelled in the meantime.
- **Give up eventually.** A job that fails every time is a **poison message**. After a few attempts, move it to a dead-letter stream, `roombook:jobs:email:dead`, and alert someone, so it doesn't fail forever.

In Spring, the worker is the same application started with a **profile**, a name you switch on at startup, like `--spring.profiles.active=worker`. A bean marked `@Profile("worker")` exists only when that profile is on, so only the worker process has the `EmailWorker` bean, as the first example shows. Its `@Scheduled` method, which needs `@EnableScheduling` on a configuration class, reads up to 10 jobs, waiting up to 5 seconds when there are none, and acknowledges each one it finishes. Spring Data Redis also has a `StreamMessageListenerContainer` that runs the polling loop for you. For retries, schedules, and a dashboard built in, Spring teams use JobRunr, or a broker through Spring AMQP or Spring for Apache Kafka.

## Live updates on every instance

The availability page should update itself when someone books, without the visitor reloading. The API styles lesson picked SSE for that: the browser opens `GET /v1/rooms/1/events` and keeps it open, and the server writes an `availability` event whenever a slot changes. With several instances, though, the visitor's stream sits on one instance, and the booking can arrive on another.

Redis **pub/sub** connects them. `SUBSCRIBE channel` makes a connection a listener on a channel, and `PUBLISH channel message` delivers a message to every connection listening at that moment. Each instance subscribes to the rooms its visitors are watching. Whichever instance commits a booking publishes to `roombook:rooms:1:events`, and every instance with a visitor on room 1 writes the event to that visitor's stream.

```diagram redis-pubsub-fanout
One instance publishes, and Redis hands the message to every instance that subscribed.
```

In step 1, instance C commits a booking and publishes. In step 2, Redis delivers the message to instances A and B, which subscribed for their visitors, and in step 3 each writes it down its open SSE streams. The publisher first takes the event's number from `INCR roombook:rooms:1:seq`, so every instance sends the same `id:` for it.

Pub/sub is fire and forget: a message reaches whoever is subscribed at that instant, and is never stored. That suits live updates, since a visitor who missed one, say while reconnecting, loads availability fresh. It doesn't suit jobs, which is why those go in a stream.

In Spring, the controller returns an `SseEmitter`, and a `RedisMessageListenerContainer` bean does the subscribing, as the second example shows. The container carries every channel on one Redis connection, and each visitor's listener is added for its room and removed when the emitter completes.

Every part of this lesson leans on another server answering in time: Redis, the email provider, the database. The next lesson, Timeouts, Retries, Idempotency, and Circuit Breakers, is about what to do when one doesn't.

examples.title: The email worker
examples.prompt: `EmailWorker` in the `jobs` package. It exists only when the app starts with `--spring.profiles.active=worker`, and the bookings service adds jobs through `EmailJobs`, which calls `opsForStream().add`.
examples.explanation: The constructor creates the group once, starting from the beginning of the stream (`ReadOffset.from("0")`), and a second worker's attempt fails because the group exists, which is fine. `read` with `ReadOffset.lastConsumed()` sends `XREADGROUP` with `">"`, asking for jobs no one in the group has received, up to 10, waiting up to 5 seconds. Each job is acknowledged only after the email went out. A failure is logged and left pending, for `XAUTOCLAIM` or a retry later. `fixedDelay = 100` starts the next read 100 milliseconds after the last one returns.

examples.title: An SSE stream fed by pub/sub
examples.prompt: `RoomEventsController` in the `rooms` package. A `RedisMessageListenerContainer` bean, built from the connection factory, does the subscribing.
examples.explanation: The emitter stays open for up to 30 minutes, then the browser reconnects, and the first event only sets `reconnectTime`, which writes `retry: 5000`. The listener is a lambda that the container calls with each message from the room's channel. It reads the `id` and `data` the publisher sent, and `SseEmitter.event()` writes them as one event named `availability`. `onCompletion` removes the listener when the stream ends for any reason. After a booking commits, a `@TransactionalEventListener` takes the next id with `increment` and calls `convertAndSend` to publish.

recap:
- A cache keeps a copy of an answer somewhere fast, and a shared one like Redis keeps one copy for every instance.
- Redis keeps keys in memory, runs one command at a time so each is atomic, and can expire any key with a TTL.
- Pick the data type for the job: strings for JSON and counters, hashes for objects, sorted sets for ordered data, streams for jobs.
- Cache-aside checks Redis first, fills it on a miss, and treats a Redis failure as a miss.
- Delete a cached copy after the commit, keep a TTL as the safety net, and let the database make every decision that must be right.
- Sessions and rate-limit counters live in Redis so every instance sees the same ones, and a limit answers 429 with Retry-After.
- Jobs go in a stream read by a consumer group and acknowledged after the work, so they must be safe to run twice.
- Pub/sub fans live updates out to every instance, and anything that mustn't be lost goes in a stream instead.
